Shankha 屬氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 423.11: The shankha is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.111.2, an end-blown conch horn of India in South Asia. The source names no composers or pieces; it can be heard mainly in Hindu temples and in household worship, above all at the arati lamp offering, and it is also used in funeral processions in Tamil Nadu. In the past it served as a war horn to call companions together, and it appears in the tradition of Sikh warriors, the Nihang Sikhs still blowing it at the evening arati and at Hola Mohalla. Its sound is the high, piercing horn call made by air passing through the spiral of the shell.

Its timbre is bright and strongly carrying, with a warm nasal edge, and is usually accompanied by a natural breathiness and subtle overtones. Its range is fairly limited, mostly in the middle and lower register, and the volume can change greatly with how hard it is blown. Its resonance is quite natural: the sound waves spiral and are amplified inside the shell, which produces an enveloping sound. Against the precision and polish of modern brass, the shankha sounds rougher and more ethereal; against the trombone it is less refined but has an older, more desolate air. Its particular resonance makes it highly recognisable in religious ritual, and it can convey a deep spiritual force.

In Hindu scriptures such as the Bhagavad Gita the conch is held sacred, above all as the emblem Vishnu guards. In ancient Indian warfare the conch was blown as a horn to give the signal for battle, and its sound stood for a sacred summons. As Hindu belief developed, the conch gradually became a purely religious instrument, blown at temple rites, weddings and important ceremonies. Its deep cultural meaning — standing for fame, long life, prosperity and purification — makes it a central element of Hindu art and religious life. As Hinduism spread to Southeast and East Asia, the conch's religious meaning spread with it, and it stands as an important witness to the reach of Indian civilisation.

The shankha is an end-blown shell horn from South Asia, an aerophone, classification number 423.111.2. Its body is a conch shell, long-oval or conical in outline and hollow inside; to play it a hole is drilled near the tip at the top of the shell, and the air passing through the spiral chamber gives a high, piercing sound. In the past it was a military horn to call companions together; today it is mostly blown in Hindu temples and household worship, at lamp offerings, and it is also used in funeral processions in Tamil Nadu; Sikh warriors and the Nihang Sikhs also use it before battle or in the evening hymns.
樂器材質以海螺殼為主，來源指出取自印度洋及周邊海域的海螺，殼面瓷質、堅硬、有光澤: The instrument is made mainly of conch shell; the source says the shells come from the Indian Ocean and neighbouring waters, their surface porcelain-like, hard, glossy and slightly translucent, hollow within; any suitable conch shell can be used, with a hole drilled at the top as the blowhole. The sounding body is the shell itself and the blowhole, and the source does not mention a reed, membrane or any other added part.
